title: Pharmacological topics of interest for young people: misinformation on TikTok is common
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of 121 publicly accessible TikTok posts (German and English) retrieved via 25 pharmacology-related hashtags and filtered for the highest number of likes. Every post was coded binary for the presence of misinformation, defined as 'contradiction to established scientific literature or clinical guidelines' and checked against PubMed, medical literature or other reliable sources. The paper reports that 32% of the 121 posts contained misinformation - a CONTENT share with an explicit denominator and an external (published-evidence) ground truth.

estimates.country: Not stated (posts in German and English; authors based at Hannover Medical School, Germany)
estimates.date: Not reported; views and likes were 'collected over a period of several weeks'. Manuscript received 11 April 2025, accepted 2 August 2025, published online 14 November 2025
estimates.measure_type: % of pharmacology-related TikTok posts containing medically related misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 32% of 121 posts (stated as 'Sixty-eight percent of 121 posts did not present any misinformation. Thirty-two percent of videos contained some form of medically related misinformation.')
estimates.denominator: 121 publicly accessible TikTok posts in German and English, found via the TikTok search function on 25 pharmacology-related hashtags (birth control, estrogen, Viagra, testosterone, steroids, opioids, weed, cbd, thc, ecstasy, lsd, fentanyl awareness and others) and then filtered for the highest number of likes
estimates.definition: Post coded 1 on the binary 'presence of incorrect information' parameter: a pharmacological or medical claim contradicting established scientific literature or clinical guidelines, checked against PubMed, medical literature or other reliable sources such as medical journals
estimates.misinfo_def: Misinformation - Contradiction to established scientific literature or clinical guidelines
estimates.source_quote: Thirty-two percent of videos contained some form of medically related misinformation.
estimates.page_loc: Results and discussion, 'Misinformation' subsection, p. 5905; repeated in the Abstract ('Thirty-two percent of posts contained misinformation') and in the Conclusions ('With 32% of misinformation present')
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Claims in each video were compared against PubMed, medical literature or other reliable sources such as medical journals, i.e. published evidence as the ground truth. RELIABILITY IS WEAK AND SELF-ACKNOWLEDGED: 'The reliability of our findings may be reduced because of the initial classification of misinformation by one coder. Future studies should include inter-coder testing.' No kappa, no double coding, binary outcome only.
estimates.moderator_quote: The initial classification of misinformation was performed by established medical literature. To evaluate the presence of incorrect information, the content was analysed by comparing the claims made with information on PubMed, in medical literature, or other reliable sources like medical journals. Only pharmacological and medical-related claims were analysed.
estimates.notes: Value stated verbatim three times (Abstract, Results, Conclusions) so the number itself is secure. Two cautions for an adjudicator. (a) The paper never prints the COUNT of misinformation posts; 32% of 121 = 38.7, so the reported percentage is rounded and the exact numerator is unrecoverable (R8 therefore forbids reconstructing a count). Occupational-group counts of misinformation videos (influencers 21, podcasts 9, unknown/no expertise 8) sum to at least 38 but overlap, because 'some creators were assigned several subcategories'. (b) denom_selection = curated because the search results were deliberately filtered for the highest number of likes - the authors flag this as selection bias: 'Since this paper focused specifically on popular posts and the number of likes was filtered, less popular posts with different quality of information may not have been found.' denom_scope = topical (a multi-issue but wholly pharmacological keyword corpus). breadth coded 'false' from the formal Table 1 definition (contradiction to established literature), but note the authors also counted over-generalisations that are not literally false (their LSD-addiction example: 'not only false claims but also generalisations can have dangerous consequences'), which widens the numerator slightly towards 'misleading'. QUOTE NOTE: source_quote is the second half of the reported pair; the first half, 'Sixty-eight percent of 121 posts did not present any misinformation.', is hyphenated across a line break in the extracted .txt ('mis-/information') and so is not a contiguous string there.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) MODERATOR SUBGROUP SHARES were NOT made into rows: none of them is a country, platform or measure split, and all share the same 121-post denominator, so rows would double-count. Recorded here in full. By language: English posts 33.3%, German posts 25% (chi-square p = 0.5064, Fisher p = 0.5796) - a language split, not a country split, and the paper never names a country. By source of reference: no source 33.68%, one source 31.57%, several sources 14.29% (chi-square p = 0.5690, Fisher p = 0.6673). By animation: with moving visual animation 43.48%, without 29.59%. By terminology: common terms 32.81%, medical terms 31.58%. By active ingredient (only ingredients mentioned more than five times): opioids 16.67%, ulipristal acetate 20%, testosterone/derivatives 22.23%, fentanyl 23.81%, levonorgestrel 28.57%, sildenafil 28.57%, LSD 30%, MDMA 30.77%, cannabis 38.46%, estrogen/gestagen 41.38%, cocaine 50% (chi-square p = 0.8136; the authors warn that videos mentioning several ingredients cannot be assigned to one, so these overlap). By occupational group the paper gives only COUNTS of misinformation posts, not within-group percentages (influencers 21, podcasts 9, unknown/no expertise 8; chi-square p = 0.0191, Fisher p = 0.0180, the only significant association with misinformation) - within-group denominators are not printed in the text, so no derivable share. 2) HIGH-ENGAGEMENT SUBSET: 'Posts in both categories showed 67% misinformation. All posts in both categories were created by influencers' (the highly-liked and highly-commented posts of Tables 6 and 7). Not extracted: the size of that subset is not stated in the text, so there is no usable denominator. Related: 'In our sample, 8 out of 10 most viewed posts were created by people without expertise with a range from 6,200,000 to 17,000,000 views... Four of these videos contained misinformation' - 4/10 of the most-viewed posts, an unstably small purposive subset, not extracted. 3) NO CONCENTRATION row: the paper reports view/like correlations (r = 0.8984, R-squared = 0.8070 for likes on views; r = 0.6732, R-squared = 0.4532 for comments) and a highly skewed view distribution, but never a top-X%-of-posts-accounted-for-Y%-of-views statement, so R1 is not met. 4) NOT MISINFORMATION SHARES, so not extracted: advertisement present in 11/121 (9%) of posts, and by group pharmacists 3 (42.86%), influencers 11 (20.76%, note this count exceeds the total of 11 advertisement posts in the text - an internal inconsistency in the paper), unknown/no expertise 1 (4.76%); source of reference one 19 (16%), several 7 (6%), none 95 (78%) - note the Abstract says 76% for no source while the Results say 78%, a further internal inconsistency; occupational-group composition (influencers 53, doctors 25, unknown/no expertise 21 of 121); ingredient frequencies (estrogen/gestagen 29, cannabis 26, fentanyl 21; illicit drugs 66 mentions, sex hormones 45, MOR-agonists 12); source use by group (news channel several sources 37.5%, doctor no source 80%, chi-square p = 0.003). 5) FIGURES CITED FROM OTHER PAPERS were excluded per R8, notably Baghdadi et al. 2023 on 166 COVID-19 TikTok videos (22% moderate-level and 11% high-level misinformation), Ricke and Seifert 2024 (63% of supplement posts contained discount codes; two-thirds exceeded maximum dosage recommendations), Chu et al. 2017 (92% used the internet for health information in the last 12 months, 97% choose the internet first), and McCashin and Murphy 2023 (32.5% of US TikTok users aged 10-19). 6) DATE OF DATA COLLECTION IS NOT REPORTED anywhere in the text; year was set to the publication year 2025 as instructed, and the true collection window is likely 2024-early 2025 given the 11 April 2025 submission. 7) COUNTRY is not stated; coded Global because only a language restriction (German and English) applies. 8) Figures 2-13 are images and could not be read; every value used here is stated verbatim in the running prose.

rob.design: Self-described pilot cross-sectional content analysis. Sampling: TikTok's own search function on 25 predefined pharmacology hashtags, results then filtered for the highest number of likes ('The use of popularity filters was chosen intentionally to reflect the highest influence and relevancy for users'); final sample 121 publicly accessible videos in German and English; no sampling frame size or screening flow is given (Fig. 1 is an unreadable flowchart), and no data-collection date is reported. Coding: 13 parameters recorded in Excel; misinformation coded as a binary outcome by comparing claims against PubMed, medical literature or other reliable sources. Reliability: NONE established - the authors state 'The reliability of our findings may be reduced because of the initial classification of misinformation by one coder. Future studies should include inter-coder testing.' Analysis: chi-square and Fisher's exact tests plus linear regression in GraphPad Prism. Author-declared limitations: small sample precludes general conclusions; popularity filtering introduces selection bias; binary misinformation coding may oversimplify; videos mentioning several drugs cannot be assigned to one ingredient; views/likes collected over several weeks so cross-video comparability is limited; one video was deleted during the study so its view count is missing. Two internal numerical inconsistencies noted above (advertisement counts by group; 76% vs 78% for no source of reference).
